notes.meaning: Now the list narrows to Abraham's family. All the other nations have been left behind. Isaac is named first, though he was younger, because he was the son of God's promise and carried on God's covenant (His binding promise-agreement with Abraham). Matthew Henry adds that this does not mean no one outside Abraham's family ever found favour with God.

Ishmael's line comes first. His twelve sons became heads of twelve tribes. This shows God keeping His word to Abraham that Ishmael would become a great nation with twelve princes (Genesis 17:20). Older writers linked these names to later Arab tribes, such as Nebaioth with the Nabataeans.

Next come Abraham's sons by Keturah, and some of their sons. Keturah is called a concubine. Adam Clarke explains this meant a wife of second rank, not a concubine in our modern sense. Her children were sent away from Isaac, the heir (Genesis 25:6). They became wandering tribes in Arabia and Syria, and Midian became the best known of them.

The writer repeats that Abraham was Isaac's father, just as Genesis 25:19 does, and then names Isaac's two sons. Esau and Israel (Jacob) are both listed, but only Israel was chosen to carry the covenant. Esau's line is given first. Israel's long story follows in the next chapter.
These are Esau's five sons, born to him by three different wives in Canaan. The line not chosen is usually listed before the chosen one. Even so, God kept His word to make Esau into a nation.

These are Esau's grandsons through his son Eliphaz. Timna was Eliphaz's concubine, and she was the mother of Amalek (Genesis 36:12). The writer shortens what Genesis says, because his readers already knew it. Amalek's descendants later became one of Israel's most stubborn enemies.
These are more of Esau's grandsons, through his son Reuel. Older writers tried to link names like Reuel and Shammah with later Arab tribes.

Seir was not from Esau's family. He was a prince of the Horites, the people who first lived on Mount Seir. His family is listed because Esau's people married into it and took over the land. Those who did not join with Esau's people were destroyed (Deuteronomy 2:12).

The list of Seir's family goes on with the sons of Lotan. It also mentions his sister Timna, the one woman named among Seir's descendants. She may be the same Timna who bore Amalek to Eliphaz (v. 36).

The list goes on with the rest of Seir's grandsons. The names match Genesis 36:20-30, apart from a few small spelling changes. Matthew Henry says spelling and pronunciation simply change over time, just as English spelling has. After Esau's people arrived, the land held twenty tribes: thirteen from Esau and seven from Seir.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: One critical scholar argued that the chronicler arranged the names in verses 28-42 to make seventy tribes, matching the seventy nations from Noah. Keil and Delitzsch count only sixty-nine names that way and reject the idea.

notes.meaning: Edom had kings long before Israel did. The list shows God keeping His promise that kings would come from Esau. Eight kings ruled one after another, until David later conquered Edom. Bela is the first king. His name, 'Bela son of Beor', sounds strikingly like 'Balaam son of Beor', and some older writers linked the two.

Jobab came from Bozrah, which became Edom's chief city. Later the prophets used the name Bozrah to stand for all of Edom. Some older writers thought Jobab was Job, but Adam Clarke notes the two names are spelled quite differently in Hebrew.
Husham came from the land of Teman, a region named after Esau's grandson (v. 36). In this whole list, no son ever follows his father as king. Each king comes from a different family and place.
Hadad is remembered for defeating Midian in the land of Moab. Adam Clarke says nothing more is known about this war. The note shows that a king could be remembered for a great deed.
Samlah came from yet another town, Masrekah. Because the throne kept moving between families, it seems Edom's kings were chosen rather than born to rule.
Shaul came from Rehoboth. The older wording says 'by the river', which is understood as the Euphrates. An old Jewish paraphrase calls it a great city on the banks of the Euphrates.
Baal-hanan son of Achbor is the next king. Once again, the new king is not the son of the king before him.

This last Hadad is called Hadar in Genesis. Keil and Delitzsch think a copyist made a small slip. The city's name, Pau or Pai, is just said a little differently. His wife's family name, Me-zahab, can mean 'waters of gold'.

Genesis does not record this king's death, because he was probably still alive in Moses' day. By the time Chronicles was written, he had long been dead, so his death is added. The words that follow may mean chiefs took over from the kings. Keil and Delitzsch think it more likely the chiefs simply ruled alongside them.

The list of Edom's chiefs ends the chapter. These may really be the names of the places where the chiefs lived, such as 'the chief of Timna'. That would explain why some names belong to women. Matthew Henry and John Wesley invite us to remember how many people have lived, made their mark and passed away. Our own time is short, so may we be known as the Lord's people.
